name: Design a DDoS Protection and Web Application Firewall Service
intent: Put a shield in front of customers' websites that absorbs floods of junk traffic, tells attackers from real people, and still lets every real visitor through.
codeTitle: an edge shield with anomaly-scored WAF rules and a baseline detector
finalIntro: A real visitor and a bot reaching the same shop while an attack is going on.
prompt: Design an edge service that protects customers' websites from denial-of-service attacks and common web attacks. Customers point their domain at it, traffic from visitors goes through it, and only clean traffic reaches the customer's own servers (the origin). Attacks range from hundreds of gigabits per second of junk packets to slow trickles of cleverly shaped requests, and real visitors must keep shopping throughout.
functional: Absorb volumetric attacks on the network and transport layers, such as SYN floods and UDP amplification
Stop application-layer floods of HTTP requests, including ones that come from hundreds of thousands of addresses
Serve static and cacheable content from the edge so most requests never reach the origin
Score clients as human or bot, and challenge the doubtful ones
Apply web application firewall (WAF) rules against injection, cross-site scripting and path traversal, with rules a customer can tune
Let customers set their own rate limits and rules, and see what was blocked and why
nonFunctional: Absorb attacks of several terabits per second without the customer's site noticing
Add under 5 ms of latency for a normal request, and nothing for a cache hit
Detect a new attack and mitigate it automatically within seconds, with no person in the loop
Block less than 0.1% of real requests by mistake, and make every block explainable
Origins must be unreachable except through the edge
The shield itself must never become the single point of failure: it keeps working if one site, or its control plane, fails

firstAttempt.text: The customer's servers sit on a public address behind one load balancer and one firewall. A few rules in the firewall block known bad addresses, a rate limit slows any single address that sends too much, and an operator watches the graphs and adds rules by hand when the site slows down.
limits: The internet link into the data centre is a few gigabits per second, and a flood of hundreds of gigabits fills it before any rule can run
A botnet of 20,000 addresses, each sending a few requests per second, defeats a per-address limit, because each looks like an ordinary visitor
Every request, however pointless, costs the origin a database query, a template render and a worker
A person adding rules takes minutes to hours, and an attack can finish or change shape in that time
A rule tight enough to stop the attack blocks shoppers who share an office address or open a page that loads thirty files
Once attackers know the origin address, any shield in front of it can be bypassed

steps.title: Announce one address from hundreds of sites (anycast)
steps.problem: A flood of hundreds of gigabits per second simply fills the link into the customer's data centre. No rule on the servers can help once the pipe is full, and one site can never be big enough.
steps.fix: Announce the same IP addresses from hundreds of points of presence around the world. The internet's routing sends each client to the nearest one, so an attack from a botnet spread across the world is split into many small attacks, each landing on the site closest to the bots. Each site has its own links and machines, and the capacity of the whole network, many terabits per second, stands behind each customer. A site that is overwhelmed can stop announcing a customer's addresses, and the traffic moves to the next nearest site. At the entrance of each site, filters work on packets: spoofed or malformed packets are dropped, UDP to ports no customer uses is dropped (which removes most amplification traffic, such as DNS, NTP and memcached replies that nobody asked for), SYN cookies answer a SYN flood without keeping any state, and a limit on connections per source keeps one address from holding thousands of slots.
steps.tradeoff: The attack meets a network built to be bigger than any one attack, and the filters are cheap per packet. The network costs a lot to build and run, so the service only makes sense for many customers sharing it. Attacks are not evenly spread, so a single site can still be hit harder than its share, and a routing change in the middle of a connection can send later packets to a different site.

steps.title: End connections at the edge and cache what you can
steps.problem: Even a small flood of valid requests would cost the origin a worker and a database query each, and most of the requests are for pages that are the same for everyone.
steps.fix: Each point of presence ends the visitor's TCP and TLS connection itself and runs a reverse proxy, so the origin only sees requests that the proxy decides to forward, over a few long-lived connections. A slow client that trickles bytes ties up only a cheap connection slot at the edge, which has a timeout. Static files and cacheable pages are kept in memory and on disk at the edge, so a hit never reaches the origin, and when a hundred requests ask for the same missing page at once, only one is sent to the origin and the others wait for its answer. The cache key is normalized, so a random query string that the page ignores does not turn every request into a miss.
steps.tradeoff: Most real traffic and a good share of attack traffic is answered at the edge for almost nothing. Pages that are personal or change every second cannot be cached, and those are the ones an attacker aims for, with search queries and logins. A stale cache can show old content, and a poorly chosen key can serve one user's page to another.

steps.title: Rate-limit clients and score how human they look
steps.problem: A botnet of 20,000 addresses sending 6 requests per second each is 120,000 requests per second, but every single address looks like an ordinary visitor. A limit per address low enough to stop it also blocks the people behind a company network.
steps.fix: Limit by more than the address. The edge builds a fingerprint from the TLS handshake, the order and set of HTTP headers, the HTTP version, the user agent and the behaviour over time, such as whether the client fetches the page's images and scripts, and counts requests per fingerprint and per session as well as per IP. A bot-score model combines these signals with the reputation of the address and returns a score from 0 to 100. Clearly human clients pass, clearly bad ones are blocked, and the doubtful middle gets a challenge: a short proof of work (a small puzzle the client must compute) or a browser check that a real browser solves without a person noticing, and a plain script cannot. The per-address limit is kept as a safety net, set well above the peak of a busy office.
steps.tradeoff: Floods that look like many separate people are stopped without a rule for each attacker. The scores are probabilities, and a challenge costs real visitors a moment, and some leave or fail it, around 3% in the model, so it is not left on all the time. Attackers use real browser farms to pass challenges, and it never ends.

steps.title: Apply WAF rules by adding up points
steps.problem: Attacks that fit one request, such as SQL injection, scripts in a form field and paths that climb out of the web root, need no flood at all. A single hard-coded rule per attack either misses variants or blocks real traffic.
steps.fix: A set of rules inspects the path, the query, the headers and the body. Each rule that matches adds points to the request's anomaly score, and the request is blocked at a threshold. A signature like 'union select' adds a lot, a double dash in a comment box adds 1, and a missing user agent adds 2, so one weak signal is only logged and several together are blocked. New rules and customer changes start in log-only mode, where the WAF records what it would have blocked, and are promoted after the false positives have been read and fixed. Customers can add exceptions for routes where their application legitimately sends code, such as a forum for programmers. Managed rule sets are updated centrally when a new vulnerability is published, which gives protection before the customer has patched.
steps.tradeoff: Scoring makes the false-positive rate adjustable, and log-first deployment finds mistakes before they cost sales. A strict setting stops more, and in the model a strict WAF wrongly blocks about 5% of real requests, against 1% for a balanced one. A WAF cannot protect against flaws in business logic, and attackers keep encoding payloads to slip below the threshold.

steps.title: Make the origin reachable only through the edge
steps.problem: If an attacker learns the origin's real address, from old DNS records, an email header or a certificate log, they can send the flood straight to it, and every defence at the edge is skipped.
steps.fix: Remove the origin's public door. A small agent next to the origin opens an outbound, encrypted tunnel to the nearest points of presence, so the origin needs no open inbound port at all. Where a tunnel is not possible, the origin's firewall allows only the edge's published address ranges and requires a client certificate (mutual TLS) or a secret header on every request, and the old addresses are changed after the shield is in place. The edge also rate-limits what it forwards, and sends traffic to a healthy origin from a pool, retrying at another when one fails.
steps.tradeoff: Attacks can no longer go around the shield, and the origin can be small because it sees only filtered traffic. The tunnel and the edge become a dependency for every visitor, so a second path and a health check are needed, and the origin cannot simply be reached for debugging from anywhere.

steps.title: Detect attacks from baselines and mitigate them automatically
steps.problem: Attacks start without warning and change shape, and an operator who reads graphs takes minutes. A flash sale also looks like a flood. Wrongly declaring an attack blocks the customer's best day.
steps.fix: Every point of presence reports rates, error ratios, cache hit ratios and origin latency every second to a control plane. For each customer the detector learns a baseline of the normal level and its spread, and raises an alarm when a measure stays above the baseline by several deviations for a couple of seconds and the origin also shows strain. While it is alarmed it stops learning, so the attack does not become the new normal. It then escalates in steps: tighten the per-fingerprint limits, raise the WAF threshold sensitivity, and finally challenge every client with no good reputation. Rules are pushed to every site in seconds, expire by themselves when the signal returns to normal, and each step records the traffic it blocked and the sample of requests that caused it, so a customer can see why. A kill switch lets a person turn off any automatic action, and the data plane keeps enforcing the last rules if the control plane is down.
steps.tradeoff: Mitigation happens in seconds without a person, and the extra friction applies only while the attack lasts. Detection is the delay: in the model it takes 8 seconds of overload plus 4 to push the rule, and during that time the origin takes the damage. Always-on protection avoids the wait but charges real visitors all the time, and thresholds that are too sensitive cause false alarms.

failures.scenario: A real flash sale makes traffic jump to 10 times normal
failures.impact: The detector sees a rate far above baseline and, if it cannot tell the difference, challenges thousands of eager customers and loses sales on the best day of the year.
failures.answer: Alarm only when the rate is high and the quality of the traffic is poor: many unfamiliar fingerprints, a falling cache hit ratio, a rise in 4xx responses and origin latency. A customer can announce an event in advance to widen the baseline. The first escalation steps only slow down clients with a bad score, and the challenge is the last step, not the first.

failures.scenario: A new WAF rule blocks a legitimate form
failures.impact: Customers of a forum for programmers cannot post code containing words like 'select' and '--', and nobody notices until sales or posts drop.
failures.answer: New and changed rules start in log-only mode and are promoted after the logged would-be blocks are reviewed. Scores add up, so one weak match does not block. Every block has a rule id and a sample, a customer can add an exception for a route in seconds, and a rule that blocks an unusual share of the customer's traffic is rolled back by itself.

failures.scenario: An attacker finds the origin's real address
failures.impact: A flood sent straight to the origin bypasses the shield, and the edge cannot help.
failures.answer: The origin accepts connections only from the tunnel or the edge's address ranges with mutual TLS, so packets from anywhere else are dropped at its network boundary. The real address is changed when the shield is first deployed, and old DNS records and certificates that expose it are removed. For a very large flood aimed at the origin's link, the upstream provider also filters traffic that does not come from the edge.

failures.scenario: A large point of presence loses power in the middle of an attack
failures.impact: Its share of the traffic, and its share of the attack, has to go somewhere, and the next nearest site may be overloaded as a result.
failures.answer: Routing moves clients to the next nearest sites within seconds, and every site is kept at a modest average load so it can take on a neighbour's share. Sites withdraw their announcements before they saturate, so that traffic is shed gradually and not all at once. Rules live in every site, so mitigation continues unchanged.

failures.scenario: The control plane is attacked or unavailable
failures.impact: New rules cannot be pushed, and the edge might fail open or closed.
failures.answer: The data plane keeps enforcing the last rules it received and can make local decisions with per-site rate limits. Rule distribution is separate from request handling and is signed, replicated and rolled out gradually. A customer's last known good configuration is cached at every site.

alternatives.title: Where to absorb volumetric attacks

options.name: Buy more bandwidth at the origin
options.pro: Simple and under the customer's control
options.con: Attacks are far larger than any one customer can afford, and capacity sits idle between attacks

options.name: On-demand scrubbing centres
options.pro: Traffic is diverted to a big cleaning site only during an attack, so it costs less
options.con: Diverting by routing takes minutes, adds latency and can drop connections

options.name: Always-on anycast edge
options.pro: No diversion delay, and capacity is shared by every customer
options.con: Expensive to build, and a small share of capacity is lost to uneven geography

alternatives.pick: Always-on anycast edge, with scrubbing centres for the largest events and for customers who only protect a network range.

alternatives.title: How to tell bots from people

options.name: Per-IP rate limit
options.con: Misses a botnet where each address is slow, and blocks offices that share one address

options.name: Fingerprints and a bot score
options.pro: Catches clients that behave like scripts, whatever their address
options.con: Needs a model and fresh data, and the scores are probabilities

options.name: A challenge for everyone
options.con: Costs every real visitor a moment, and farms of real browsers still pass

alternatives.pick: Scores first, a challenge only for the doubtful or when an attack is detected, and a per-IP limit as a safety net.

alternatives.title: How to score WAF rules

options.name: Block on any signature match
options.con: Many false positives, since single keywords appear in normal text

options.name: Anomaly scoring with a threshold
options.pro: Weak signals add up, and the strictness is a single number
options.con: The score needs tuning, and attackers can try to stay below it

options.name: A model trained on the customer's traffic
options.con: Needs time to learn, is hard to explain and can be trained by an attacker

alternatives.pick: Anomaly scoring with log-first rollout, and a learned model as one input to the score.

alternatives.title: When to challenge

options.name: Always on
options.con: A permanent cost for real visitors

options.name: Only when an attack is detected
options.pro: Real visitors are inconvenienced only when it is needed
options.con: The first seconds of an attack are not covered

options.name: Only on suspicious clients
options.con: Depends on the quality of the score

alternatives.pick: Suspicious clients always, everyone while an attack is confirmed, and a customer can choose always-on for a sensitive route such as login.

quiz.question: A shop's servers sit behind a 10 Gbps internet link, one load balancer and one firewall. A UDP flood of 300 Gbps arrives, and the firewall rules cannot even be reached. Which design change addresses the cause?
options: Announce the same addresses from hundreds of sites (anycast), so the flood is split among them and each site filters packets
Buy a 100 Gbps link and a larger firewall, so that the link can carry the attack while the firewall drops it
Add a rule on the firewall that drops all UDP traffic from addresses outside the shop's main country
Add a per-address rate limit on the load balancer, set low enough to slow every source sending the flood
quiz.explanation: The pipe is full before any rule runs, so the fix is capacity far larger than any attack and spread over the world. Even 100 Gbps would be filled by 300 Gbps. Firewall and load balancer rules sit behind the full link and cannot run.

quiz.question: A botnet of 20,000 addresses sends 6 requests per second each, which is 120,000 requests per second to a search page. A per-address limit of 5 requests per second would stop it, but it also blocks offices where 50 people share one address. What is the best approach?
options: Challenge every client with a browser check on every request, since that stops simple bots at the cost of a short wait for people
Keep the 5 requests per second limit and ask the affected offices to register their address ranges so they can be exempted
Count requests per fingerprint and session as well as per address, score each client, and challenge only the doubtful
Scale the origin to 120,000 requests per second, so that every request is served and nothing real is blocked
quiz.explanation: Each address looks like an ordinary visitor, so the signals must be richer than the address: TLS and header fingerprints, behaviour, and reputation. Challenging only the doubtful middle keeps the cost to real people low. Exempting registered offices leaves the limit blocking every other shared address, and needs manual upkeep. A challenge for all costs every visitor, in the model about 3% leave, and scaling the origin pays for every pointless request.

quiz.question: A customer's flash sale makes traffic jump to 10 times its baseline. A detector that sees the rate far above normal could treat it as an attack and challenge thousands of eager shoppers. Which design avoids that?
options: Alarm at several deviations above baseline for two seconds, then challenge every client with no good reputation at once, which is the quickest way to stop a flood
Switch protection off during announced sales, since a sale has no attackers and the extra checks only slow buyers
Raise the stored baseline to the new level after any jump, so the same rate is no longer seen as unusual
Alarm only when the rate is high and the traffic looks poor, with unfamiliar fingerprints, a falling cache hit ratio and rising origin latency
quiz.explanation: Volume alone cannot tell a sale from a flood, so the quality of the traffic is checked as well, and friction rises in steps. Challenging at once costs real sales. Switching off leaves the best day open to a real attack, and learning the jump as the new normal lets an attack become normal too.
